title: while(flag){} never terminates — JVM caching/hoisting, volatile fix
shortTitle: Why does while(flag){} never terminate without volatile?

s1_definition.profdef: Without `volatile`, the JIT compiler may **hoist** the flag read out of the loop — it sees that `flag` is never modified WITHIN the loop body and optimizes `while(flag) { work(); }` into `if (flag) while(true) { work(); }`. The flag is read ONCE and cached in a CPU register. Even when another thread sets `flag = false` in main memory, the loop thread NEVER reads from main memory again — it's stuck in an infinite loop using the cached `true`. This is a legal JIT optimization under the Java Memory Model because without `volatile` or `synchronized`, there's no happens-before relationship between the write and the read. `volatile` fixes this: every read MUST go to main memory, preventing hoisting and register caching.
s1_definition.analogy: A bank security guard checks the "OPEN" sign once when their shift starts. The guard writes "OPEN=true" on a STICKY NOTE (CPU register) and keeps checking their sticky note all day — never looks at the actual sign again! When the manager flips the sign to "CLOSED" at 5PM, the guard STILL reads "OPEN" from the sticky note → never locks the doors. `volatile` = the guard MUST look at the ACTUAL SIGN every time, not the sticky note. Sees "CLOSED" → locks the doors.
s1_definition.oneliner: Without volatile: JIT hoists flag read out of loop → cached in register → never sees update → infinite loop. With volatile: every read from main memory → sees update → loop exits.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Without `volatile`, the JIT compiler may **hoist** the flag read out of the loop — it sees that `flag` is never modified WITHIN the loop body and optimizes `while(flag) { work(); }` into `if (flag) while(true) { work(); }`. The flag is read ONCE and cached in a CPU register. Even when another thread sets `flag = false` in main memory, the loop thread NEVER reads from main memory again — it's stuck in an infinite loop using the cached `true`. This is a legal JIT optimization under the Java Memory Model because without `volatile` or `synchronized`, there's no happens-before relationship between the write and the read. `volatile` fixes this: every read MUST go to main memory, preventing hoisting and register caching.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** A bank security guard checks the "OPEN" sign once when their shift starts. The guard writes "OPEN=true" on a STICKY NOTE (CPU register) and keeps checking their sticky note all day — never looks at the actual sign again! When the manager flips the sign to "CLOSED" at 5PM, the guard STILL reads "OPEN" from the sticky note → never locks the doors. `volatile` = the guard MUST look at the ACTUAL SIGN every time, not the sticky note. Sees "CLOSED" → locks the doors.

**One line to remember:** Without volatile: JIT hoists flag read out of loop → cached in register → never sees update → infinite loop. With volatile: every read from main memory → sees update → loop exits.

sections.s3_banking: **Problem — The market data feed processor had a `while(running)` loop without volatile.** When the shutdown signal was sent at 5PM (`running = false`), the processor thread continued consuming market data indefinitely. At 7PM, the ops team noticed the service was still processing after-hours data → filed 2 hours of garbage trades. Investigation: JIT compiled the loop to `while(true)` because `running` was not volatile. The flag write in main memory was invisible to the loop thread's cached register. Fix: `volatile boolean running`.

sections.s5_journey:
**Step 1.** Worker thread starts `while(running)` loop. `running = true`. JIT initially interprets the bytecode — reads `running` from memory each iteration.

**Step 2.** After ~10,000 iterations, JIT compiles the hot loop to native code. Without volatile: JIT sees `running` is never modified in the loop body → optimizes: caches `running` in CPU register → effectively `while(true)`.

**Step 3.** Main thread calls `stop()` → sets `running = false` in main memory. But worker thread's register still holds `true` → loop continues forever.

**Step 4 (volatile fix).** With `volatile boolean running`: JIT is forbidden from hoisting the read. Every iteration → volatile read → goes to main memory → sees `false` → loop exits.

sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — JIT Hoisting + volatile Memory Barrier ═══

  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  CPU Architecture: Register vs Memory     │
  │                                            │
  │  CPU Register: ~0.5ns access (fastest!)    │
  │  L1 Cache:     ~1ns                        │
  │  L2 Cache:     ~3ns                        │
  │  L3 Cache:     ~10ns                       │
  │  Main Memory:  ~100ns (slowest!)           │
  │                                            │
  │  JIT optimization: keep hot variables in   │
  │  register → 200x faster than main memory!  │
  │  Legal under JMM if no happens-before.     │
  │                                            │
  │  volatile: forces read/write through to    │
  │  main memory → prevents register caching   │
  │  + inserts memory barrier instruction      │
  │  (MFENCE on x86, DMB on ARM)              │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────┘

  JIT without volatile:           JIT with volatile:
  ┌─────────────────────┐        ┌─────────────────────┐
  │ r1 = load(running)  │        │ loop:               │
  │ loop:               │        │   r1 = LOAD(running)│ ← every iteration!
  │   if r1==false goto │        │   MFENCE            │ ← memory barrier
  │     end             │        │   if r1==false goto  │
  │   doWork()          │        │     end              │
  │   goto loop         │        │   doWork()           │
  │ end:                │        │   goto loop          │
  └─────────────────────┘        └─────────────────────┘
  r1 loaded ONCE → infinite!     LOAD every iteration → sees false!
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Without `volatile`, the JIT compiler can hoist a flag read out of a loop — it caches the value in a CPU register and never reads from main memory again. `while(running)` becomes effectively `while(true)` after JIT compilation. Even though another thread sets `running = false` in main memory, the loop thread never sees it — the register holds the stale `true` value. This is a legal JIT optimization under the Java Memory Model because without a happens-before relationship (volatile, synchronized, or Lock), there's no guarantee of cross-thread visibility.

`volatile` fixes this by: (1) forbidding JIT from caching the variable in a register — every read MUST go to main memory, (2) inserting a memory barrier instruction (MFENCE on x86) that prevents instruction reordering, and (3) invalidating other CPUs' caches on write — ensuring all cores see the latest value. In banking: market feed processor with `while(running)` without volatile → continued processing 2 hours after shutdown signal → filed garbage after-hours trades. Fix: `volatile boolean running`. One keyword, critical difference.

keyPoints: JVM may cache flag in CPU register — never re-reads memory
JIT may hoist read out of loop — infinite loop
volatile forces re-read from main memory every access
